name: Microsoft Teams Essentials
tagline: Host small private video rooms and a simple team chat on user-owned infrastructure

pricing.notes: Official Teams Essentials monthly seat price with annual billing.

tiers.name: Microsoft Teams Free
tiers.limits: Group meetings up to 60 minutes and 100 participants; 1-to-1 meetings up to 30 hours; 5 GB storage per user

tiers.name: Microsoft Teams Essentials
tiers.limits: Meetings up to 30 hours and 300 participants; 10 GB storage per user
tiers.notes: $48 per user billed yearly; no public month-to-month rate

tiers.name: Microsoft 365 Business Basic
tiers.limits: Up to 300 users; meetings up to 300 participants; 1 TB storage per user
tiers.notes: $84 per user billed yearly; no public month-to-month rate on the comparison page

tiers.name: Microsoft 365 Business Standard with Copilot
tiers.limits: Up to 300 users; meetings up to 300 participants; 1 TB storage per user
tiers.notes: $282 per user billed yearly; includes desktop apps and Copilot

pricing.freeTierCaps: Group meetings: 60 minutes and 100 participants; 1-to-1 meetings: 30 hours; 5 GB storage per user
pricing.billingTerms: annual subscription with automatic renewal for the listed paid options; no public month-to-month Teams Essentials price
pricing.hiddenCosts: The $4 rate requires yearly billing. PSTN calling, Teams Phone and some advanced webinar/meeting features require other plans or add-ons.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Microsoft Teams Essentials, host small private video rooms and a simple team chat on user-owned infrastructure. The hard boundary is microsoft identity, global media, calendars, files, telephony, admin, and support, plus real-time media infrastructure and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Host small private video rooms and a simple team chat on user-owned infrastructure, issue signed room links, and keep recordings only when every participant is clearly informed.
whatYouLose: Microsoft identity, global media, calendars, files, telephony, admin, and support
ongoingBurden: TURN capacity, codecs, browsers, packet loss, scaling, recording, consent, abuse, monitoring, and incident response
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Microsoft Teams Essentials because video products survive because real-time media quality and global reliability are infrastructure businesses, not weekend interface projects. The recurring cost buys TURN capacity, codecs, browsers, packet loss, scaling, recording, consent, abuse, monitoring, and incident response, not just the visible interface.

alternatives.name: Nextcloud Hub
alternatives.desc: Team files, documents, chat and calls under one roof; you also own the roof.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Mattermost Entry
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free edition now forgets after 10,000 messages and hangs up calls at 40 minutes.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Teams Essentials plan and a small private meeting service DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Microsoft Teams Essentials in an empty repository.
Use Docker Compose, Jitsi Meet, a small Next.js 15 control panel, PostgreSQL, and TURN; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: host small private video rooms and a simple team chat on user-owned infrastructure, issue signed room links, and keep recordings only when every participant is clearly informed.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Deploy Jitsi Meet through pinned Docker images and configure a dedicated TURN service.
Build an owner panel for rooms, signed invitations, expiry, lobby mode, and participant limits.
Show connection diagnostics for camera, microphone, browser, bandwidth, and TURN reachability.
Make recording disabled by default and require an on-screen consent state for every participant.
Store room metadata and audit events, but do not store media unless explicitly enabled.
Add health checks, bandwidth dashboards, backup, restore, upgrade, and incident instructions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out a global media edge network.
Deliberately leave out public webinar scale and telephony.
Deliberately leave out regulated recording, enterprise compliance, and guaranteed support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
